claim: New Jersey law requires merchants to clearly mark the price of items either on the item or on the display where it is offered for sale (cited to https://www.njconsumeraffairs.gov/News/Brochures/Consumer-Shopping-Guide.pdf).
problem: I read all 24 pages of the cited Consumer Shopping Guide. It contains no price-marking mandate. It covers refund-policy posting, rain checks, layaway, gift cards and scams, and only advises shoppers to 'watch the cash register display to make sure the scanned price matches the advertised or posted price.' The obligation itself appears to exist, but under N.J.S.A. 56:8-2.5 (total selling price 'plainly marked' by stamp, tag, label or sign on the merchandise or where it is offered for sale) - a provision the brief does not cite. As written, a legal rule is presented as confirmed by a source that does not support it.
fix: Re-cite this fact to N.J.S.A. 56:8-2.5 (or the NJ Division of Consumer Affairs release quoting it) and drop the shopping-guide citation for the price-marking requirement. Keep the shopping guide only for what it actually says (e.g. consumers are told to check the register against the posted price).

claim: legal_privacy: 'N.J.A.C. 13:47C-3.5 sets a penalty of not less than $100 per violation, and each package in violation is a separate violation under N.J.S.A. 51:1-100' - presented as the penalty backing the NJ price/tag-accuracy obligation.
problem: The wording is quoted accurately (Cornell LII confirms it), but it is scoped to 'the provisions of this subchapter' - i.e. N.J.A.C. 13:47C Subchapter 3, NONFOODSTUFFS (firewood delivery tickets, holiday decorating materials, building-materials advertising, paper-product quantity declarations). Nothing in that subchapter concerns retail price marking of grocery items, so using 13:47C-3.5 as the price-accuracy penalty misstates the legal basis of the risk the pitch leans on.
fix: State that 13:47C-3.5 covers nonfoodstuffs packaging/quantity rules only, and either drop the $100-per-package figure or source price-marking enforcement from the Consumer Fraud Act route actually used by OWM (the two OAG settlements are the defensible citations).

fix: Replace the dead statute link with https://pub.njleg.gov/Bills/2022/PL23/266_.HTM (P.L. 2023, c.266) or the DCA NJDPA FAQ page.

claim: State v. Diaz (1998) held the video portion of a recording is outside the NJ Wiretap Act, cited to https://caselaw.findlaw.com/court/nj-superior-court-appellate-division/1193224.html.
problem: That URL returned HTTP 403, so the cited page could not be re-opened by a verifier. The holding and year are correct (308 N.J. Super. 504 (App. Div. 1998): video portion outside the Act; audio portion separately upheld under the consent provision).
fix: Swap in an openable citation (e.g. a court-opinion PDF or openjurist record for 308 N.J. Super. 504) so the claim can be checked without a paywall/block.
